title: Viral Hepatitis
path: Prevention and Control of Communicable Diseases

headings.title: Introduction to Viral Hepatitis and Types (A, B, C, D, E)
headings.content: Viral hepatitis is a systemic inflammation of the liver primarily caused by five distinct hepatotropic viruses: Hepatitis A, B, C, D, and E. As nursing students in Nigeria, understanding these classifications is crucial due to their varying epidemiological impacts, modes of transmission, and clinical outcomes. Hepatitis A virus (HAV) and Hepatitis E virus (HEV) typically cause acute, self-limiting infections and are primarily transmitted via the fecal-oral route, often through contaminated food and water supplies, which is a significant public health concern in resource-limited settings. Conversely, Hepatitis B virus (HBV), Hepatitis C virus (HCV), and Hepatitis D virus (HDV) are bloodborne pathogens transmitted through parenteral, sexual, or perinatal routes. HBV and HCV are notorious for establishing chronic infections that can lead to long-term sequelae such as cirrhosis, hepatic failure, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Hepatitis D is a defective RNA virus that can only replicate in the presence of an active Hepatitis B infection, leading to either coinfection or superinfection, which generally exacerbates disease severity. Differentiating between these viral types dictates the appropriate clinical management, infection control practices, and public health interventions required to curb transmission within Nigerian healthcare facilities and communities.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Liver Function Alterations
headings.content: The pathophysiology of viral hepatitis centers on the immune system's response to hepatocyte infection. When hepatotropic viruses invade the liver, the body's cell-mediated immune response—specifically cytotoxic T lymphocytes—attacks the infected hepatocytes, causing widespread inflammation, cellular injury, and necrosis. This hepatic inflammation disrupts normal liver architecture and impairs critical metabolic, synthetic, and excretory functions. As liver cells are destroyed, key biochemical processes fail. Alterations in carbohydrate and lipid metabolism occur, but the most clinically prominent disruptions involve bilirubin metabolism and protein synthesis. Impaired uptake, conjugation, and excretion of bilirubin lead to hyperbilirubinemia, which clinically manifests as jaundice, dark amber urine, and pale stools due to the absence of urobilinogen in the intestines. Furthermore, the liver's inability to synthesize vital proteins, particularly albumin and clotting factors (such as prothrombin), results in hypoalbuminemia leading to peripheral edema and ascites, as well as prolonged bleeding times putting the client at risk for hemorrhage. Additionally, impaired clearance of toxins like ammonia can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy. Understanding these alterations helps nursing students connect underlying cellular damage to the observable clinical signs and symptoms presented by patients.

headings.title: Modes of Transmission and Epidemiological Risk Factors
headings.content: Understanding the modes of transmission and epidemiological risk factors for viral hepatitis is essential for implementing effective infection control in Nigerian healthcare and community settings. Hepatitis A and E are spread predominantly through the fecal-oral route, heavily linked to poor sanitation, overcrowding, inadequate personal hygiene, and consumption of contaminated water or food sources like raw shellfish. In contrast, Hepatitis B, C, and D are bloodborne and transmitted through percutaneous or mucosal exposure to infectious body fluids. Major epidemiological risk factors include sharing contaminated needles or equipment among people who inject drugs, receiving unscreened blood transfusions or unsafe therapeutic injections, occupational needle-stick injuries among healthcare workers, unprotected sexual intercourse with infected partners, and vertical transmission from an infected mother to her newborn during childbirth. In sub-Saharan Africa, horizontal transmission during early childhood through breaks in the skin or mucous membranes also contributes significantly to the high endemicity of Hepatitis B. Nurses must recognize these transmission pathways to educate communities effectively, promote safe injection practices, advocate for blood safety screening, and utilize standard precautions rigorously in clinical practice to prevent nosocomial spread.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations: Acute versus Chronic Infection
headings.content: The clinical manifestations of viral hepatitis vary significantly depending on whether the infection is acute or chronic. Acute hepatitis typically progresses through three distinct phases: the pre-icteric (prodromal), icteric, and post-icteric (convalescent) phases. During the pre-icteric phase, clients often experience vague, flu-like symptoms including generalized fatigue, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, right upper quadrant abdominal discomfort, and low-grade fever. As the disease advances to the icteric phase, jaundice develops, accompanied by dark urine, clay-colored stools, and severe pruritus due to bile salt accumulation in the skin. Hepatomegaly with localized tenderness upon palpation is universally present. In the post-icteric phase, jaundice gradually resolves, and energy levels return, though fatigue may persist for weeks. Conversely, chronic infections—most commonly seen with Hepatitis B and C—are often insidious and asymptomatic for years, leading many clients to present late with complications of advanced liver disease such as ascites, peripheral edema, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, asterixis, and variceal bleeding. Recognizing these clinical trajectories allows nurses to perform accurate assessments and anticipate life-threatening complications.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Laboratory Investigations
headings.content: Diagnostic evaluation and laboratory investigations are critical for confirming viral hepatitis, identifying the specific causative agent, and assessing the degree of hepatic impairment. Serological markers and viral load assays form the cornerstone of diagnosis. For instance, anti-HAV IgM indicates an acute Hepatitis A infection, while anti-HAV IgG signifies past infection or immunity. Hepatitis B diagnosis relies on a panel of markers: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) indicates active infection, anti-HBs denotes immunity, and Hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) reflects high viral replication and infectivity. Hepatitis C is diagnosed using anti-HCV antibodies, followed by confirmatory HCV RNA PCR testing. Liver function tests (LFTs) show marked elevations in serum aminotransferases—alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST)—reflecting hepatocellular injury. Bilirubin levels (both direct and indirect) are elevated, while serum albumin and coagulation profiles (prothrombin time/INR) measure the synthetic capacity of the liver, with prolonged INR indicating severe functional decline. Imaging studies such as abdominal ultrasound help evaluate liver size, texture, and detect complications like ascites, while liver biopsy or non-invasive elastography assesses the extent of fibrosis and cirrhosis.

headings.title: Medical Management and Pharmacological Interventions
headings.content: Medical management and pharmacological interventions for viral hepatitis focus on supportive care for acute self-limiting infections and targeted antiviral therapy for chronic infections to prevent long-term complications. Acute viral hepatitis (such as uncomplicated HAV or HEV) generally requires supportive therapy, including adequate rest, intravenous or oral hydration, and a balanced diet tailored to tolerance, while strictly avoiding hepatotoxic substances like alcohol and paracetamol. For chronic Hepatitis B and C, the therapeutic goals are to suppress viral replication, halt disease progression, and prevent cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Chronic Hepatitis B is managed with nucleos(t)ide analogues such as entecavir or tenofovir, which inhibit viral polymerase, or occasionally with pegylated interferon-alpha. Chronic Hepatitis C is treated with highly effective direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) such as sofosbuvir and ledipasvir, which achieve high cure rates (sustained virological response) with minimal side effects within a relatively short treatment window of 8 to 12 weeks. In cases of end-stage liver disease or acute liver failure, evaluation for orthotopic liver transplantation becomes the definitive life-saving intervention. Nurses must monitor client adherence to complex pharmacological regimens and assess for potential side effects.

headings.title: Nursing Care and Client Education
headings.content: Nursing care and client education play a pivotal role in promoting recovery, preventing disease transmission, and improving the quality of life for clients with viral hepatitis. Nurses must implement standard and transmission-based precautions, ensuring safe handling and disposal of sharps and contaminated body fluids. For hospitalized clients experiencing acute symptoms, nursing interventions include promoting physical and psychological rest to decrease metabolic demands on the liver, managing nausea and anorexia through small, frequent, high-carbohydrate meals, and monitoring fluid and electrolyte balance. Skin care is vital to manage pruritus caused by jaundice, which can be mitigated by keeping the skin clean and cool. Client and family education is paramount: nurses must instruct the client on strictly avoiding alcohol, herbal concoctions, and over-the-counter medications like paracetamol that undergo hepatic metabolism. Education must also cover transmission prevention strategies, such as practicing meticulous hand hygiene, avoiding sharing personal care items like toothbrushes and razors, practicing safe sex, and ensuring household contacts are screened and vaccinated where appropriate. Empowering clients with this knowledge ensures compliance with therapeutic regimens and protects community health.

headings.title: Prevention, Control, and Immunization Strategies in Community Health
headings.content: Prevention, control, and immunization strategies are the most effective public health tools for reducing the burden of viral hepatitis in community health settings across Nigeria. Community health nurses lead vaccination programs, which are vital for primary prevention. Safe and effective vaccines are readily available for Hepatitis A and Hepatitis B. The Hepatitis B vaccine is a core component of the expanded program on immunization (EPI) for infants, starting with a birth dose within the first 24 hours of life followed by subsequent doses to prevent vertical and early childhood transmission. For adults at high risk, catch-up vaccination campaigns are essential. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) using Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) combined with the vaccine is administered following needle-stick injuries or perinatal exposure to non-immune individuals. Secondary and tertiary prevention strategies include public health awareness campaigns on safe sex, promoting harm reduction programs (such as needle-exchange initiatives), ensuring universal blood product screening in blood banks, enforcing stringent infection control practices in healthcare facilities, and expanding access to screening and treatment programs to reduce chronic liver disease and mortality.
